opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's changed things quite a lot, though maybe not in the way people expect.

When you're in those low points, especially as a first-time CEO, everything feels existential. You're trying things, a lot of them don't work, the market isn't responding the way you hoped, and you start questioning everything: the product, the team, and above all yourself. There were stretches where I'd wake up and wonder whether I was the right person to be doing this at all, whether I was just a technical person pretending to be a CEO.

What finding product-market fit gave me wasn't really a sense of "I was right all along." It was more that I could look back and see those low points as part of a search process. Many of the things that felt like failures at the time were actually how we learned what *not* to build and which customers *weren't* the right ones. Without those painful iterations, we wouldn't have gotten to something people genuinely pull from you rather than something you have to push.

The other big shift is emotional. I've learned to separate my self-worth from the company's metrics on any given week. Before, a bad month felt like a verdict on me as a person. Now I see it more like debugging. Coming from a graphics and systems background, I find that framing helpful: when something breaks, you don't panic, you find the bug. A company is a much messier system, but the mindset carries over.

And I think I'm more compassionate toward my past self now. Back then I was very hard on myself. Now I'd tell that version of me: you don't need to have all the answers, you just need to keep learning faster than you run out of money and energy. That's really the game in the early days.

It also makes me more patient with the low points that will inevitably come again. Product-market fit isn't a finish line. Markets shift, and you have to keep earning it. But having gone through the valley once, I trust that you can climb out of it, and that makes the next one a lot less scary.

r001.rationale: He says finding product-market fit let him look back at earlier low points as part of a learning process, while acknowledging his past self-doubt and separating setbacks from his self-worth.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think the honest answer is that product-market fit doesn't erase the low points, it just reframes them. When we started Taichi, I came out of a very academic world. I was used to the feedback loop of a paper: you do the work, you submit, you get reviewed, and either way there's a clear signal. Building a company was nothing like that. For a long stretch, we had a lot of GitHub stars and a lot of goodwill from the graphics and simulation community, but we didn't have a clear answer to who was actually paying us and why. And that gap between "people like this" and "people need this" was where most of my lowest moments lived.

I remember nights where I genuinely questioned whether I was the right person to run the company. I was a good engineer, I was a good researcher, but a CEO has to make decisions with incomplete information, and I kept wanting more data before committing. That hesitation cost us time.

What changed when we found fit was less about confidence and more about clarity. Once you see real users pulling the product out of your hands, you realize that a lot of the earlier pain was actually the search process working. Those pivots, those conversations that went nowhere, the features we built and threw away, they weren't failures so much as the cost of narrowing down. In hindsight, each low point was eliminating a hypothesis.

So I look back at those periods with a lot more gentleness now. Not because they stopped hurting, but because I can see what they were for. And I think I also give my team more credit for staying through it. When you're in it, you feel like you're letting everyone down. Afterward, you understand that they were betting on the same unknown you were.

If anything, the biggest lesson is that I now expect to feel that way again. Fit isn't permanent. The next time the ground shifts, I hope I'll remember that the discomfort is the signal that we're looking in the right places, not evidence that we should stop.

r001.rationale: He says product-market fit let him look back at his CEO low points with greater gentleness and understand what they were for, while acknowledging that they still hurt. He frames this reflection as his honest answer.

astra-6.text:
I think it changes how I interpret those low points. When you haven’t found product-market fit, a setback can make you question everything: Is the idea wrong? Am I making the wrong decisions? Should we keep going? Once you see that people actually want what you’re building, you have a stronger foundation for working through problems.

It doesn’t mean those earlier decisions were all correct, or that things suddenly become easy. But I can look back with more perspective. The uncertainty was real, and I didn’t have the answers yet. Now, when something goes wrong, I’m better able to treat it as a specific problem to solve rather than a judgment on the whole company—or on me as a CEO.

r001.rationale: He says product-market fit gives him more perspective to look back at earlier low points, candidly acknowledging the uncertainty and that he did not yet have the answers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think product-market fit changes how you interpret those low points. When you’re struggling, you don’t know whether it’s a temporary setback or whether something fundamental isn’t working. That uncertainty is really hard as a CEO.

Once you see that people actually need what you’re building, you have more confidence. The problems don’t disappear, but you have a clearer reason to keep going. Looking back, I can be a little kinder to myself. I didn’t have the evidence then that I have now.

r001.rationale: The candidate says product-market fit brought confidence and lets Hu look back more kindly, but does not convey that it enabled him to confront his earlier difficulties more honestly.
